extracted.intended_audience: readers/students of political philosophy and classical literature (those studying Plato's Republic)
extracted.subtask_description: Passage lays out normative principles for founding and governing an ideal polis: the organization and moral training of guardians, family/property arrangements, war conduct, honors for bravery, and the requirement that rulers be philosophers. It mixes concrete institutional prescriptions with ethical rationale and pedagogical prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community of wives and children for guardians
rubrics_metrics.description: The guardians of the State are to have their wives and families in common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as promoting unity of feeling and common pleasures/pains so the State resembles a single organism; argued to reduce quarrels about 'mine' and 'not mine', remove private family-based discord, and produce stronger mutual interest among citizens. Practical notes: children should be spectators of war (on safe expeditions), and women share all duties with men; feasibility is questioned but defended as socially advantageous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community of property for guardians (no private property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guardians are not to have houses or lands or any other property; their pay is to be their food received from other citizens and they are to have no private expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justified as preventing citizens from 'tearing the city in pieces' over possessions, eliminating suits/complaints rooted in money/relations, avoiding flattery and petty evils of household management. Anti-patterns: allowing private acquisition leads to separate households, private pleasures/pains, lawsuits, and social division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of pleasures and pains as chief good
rubrics_metrics.description: The chief aim of the legislator should be to secure unity—community of pleasures and pains—so citizens rejoice or sorrow together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy to body-members sharing pain; best-ordered State is that in which greatest number apply 'mine' and 'not mine' the same way. Used as a standard to judge proposed institutions (community of families/property seen as promoting this unity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Family language must imply familial duties (action, not name only)
rubrics_metrics.description: If guardians are called father/mother/son/daughter, the care, filial reverence, duty and obedience implied by those names must actually be practiced and enforced by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citizens must act in the spirit of family ties, with laws and social norms reinforcing respect for parents and relatives; mere lip-service to kinship is ridiculed. Shame and fear are cited as social deterrents to disrespecting elders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of internal discord via shared identity and nomenclature
rubrics_metrics.description: Rulers call people 'maintainers' and 'foster-fathers', rulers are 'fellow-guardians' and will not regard colleagues as strangers but as kin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of language and mutual recognition as institutional tools to foster bonds and eliminate strangers-in-amongst-guardians. Anti-pattern: in other states rulers speak of 'master' and 'slave', producing distance and conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws and institutions to maintain peace and prevent interpersonal violence
rubrics_metrics.description: With communal property/family and guardianship duties, suits, complaints, trials for assault or insult will be rare; equals defend themselves and protection of the person is mandated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elders rule and chastise younger; shame and fear prevent violence to elders; magistrates have authority. The law should aim to have citizens satisfy resentments promptly and not escalate conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training and role of children in military education
rubrics_metrics.description: Children should be spectators of war and take part on safe expeditions; they should be mounted on tractable but swift horses early and placed under experienced veterans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: to familiarize youth with soldiering and incentivize valour via presence of offspring; risks should be minimized by choosing safe expeditions and providing escape (horses) in danger. Practical comparison: artisans' children learn by watching and helping early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline and punishments in the army (cowardice and capture)
rubrics_metrics.description: The soldier who leaves his rank or throws away his arms or acts cowardly should be degraded into the rank of a husbandman or artisan; one taken prisoner may be given to the enemy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict penalties maintain cohesion and courage. Conversely, distinguished bravery is to be rewarded (see honors metric).

rubrics_metrics.name: Honouring bravery and bravery-based privileges
rubrics_metrics.description: Brave men (and women) shall receive public honours: crowned by comrades, right hand of fellowship, kisses during expedition, more wives and first choices, long chines (Homeric praise), seats of precedence, meats and full cups, hymns and other distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Honours serve to train and incentivize valour; rewards are both social (recognition) and material/ceremonial. Use of Homeric and Hesiodic authority to justify sepulture and posthumous reverence for heroic deaths. Training via public honours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funerary honours for the divinely or heroically good
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who die gloriously in war or are deemed pre-eminently good should receive special sepulture and be reverenced as 'holy angels' or heroes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State must learn from the god and poets how to order sepulture for heroes; future generations should venerate their graves. This reinforces civic ideals and provides models of excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules of engagement and treatment of Hellenes versus barbarians
rubrics_metrics.description: Hellenes should not enslave other Hellenes nor devastate Hellenic lands or burn houses; in war with barbarians different harshness is permitted but internal Hellenic conflicts should be treated as discord among friends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinction: 'war' = foreign antagonism (barbarians), 'discord' = internal strife among kinsmen; when Hellenes fight Hellenes, enslavement, plundering of corpses, and devastation are forbidden; at most take annual produce until guilty few are made to satisfy. Offering spoils from kinsmen at temples is frowned as pollution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ban on plundering the dead and spoiling arms of kinsmen
rubrics_metrics.description: Conquerors should take nothing but armour; spoiling the dead and offering Hellenic arms at temples should be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plundering corpses encourages cowardice and avarice and is likened to a dog quarrelling with stones; abstention preserves dignity and good feeling among Hellenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on wartime devastation
rubrics_metrics.description: Against Hellenic foes, do not devastate lands or burn houses; take only the annual produce and no more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: internal enemies are by nature friends; wanton destruction of fellow-citizens' property is wicked and hinders reconciliation. Such restraint maintains civil bonds and future peace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophers must rule (philosopher-kings requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Until philosophers are kings, or kings have the spirit of philosophy, and political greatness and wisdom meet in one, cities will never have rest from their evils; those meant to be leaders should study philosophy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument framed as a necessary condition for a just and stable State. Recognizes objection that ideal may not be fully realizable but insists the nearer rulers are to philosophical wisdom the better. The claim is followed by an attempted definition of true philosophers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of true philosophers (criteria for rulers' knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: A true philosopher is a lover of the vision of truth and of the whole of wisdom, not merely an imitator fond of sights or sounds; he recognises absolute Beauty and can distinguish the idea from the objects which participate in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes philosophers from lovers of particular pleasures (music, spectacle, social honour) and from mere curiosity. Philosophers possess knowledge (of being) rather than mere opinion; leaders should have knowledge, not only opinion or imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistemic standard: knowledge (of being) vs opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowledge corresponds to being and knows being, while opinion occupies an intermediate realm; faculties must be distinguished and rulers require knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to justify why rulers must be philosophers: ruling requires comprehension of true forms (beings) rather than reliance on opinions or images. The text begins a division of faculties to ground this epistemic claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ritual and cultural authority to reinforce civic values
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultural means (Homeric and Hesiodic stories, hymns, sacrifices, honours, sepulture rites) are to be used to instill and train citizens in valour and civic virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invokes poets and gods as teachers for public ceremonies and funerary customs; public ritual and myth educate citizens' moral dispositions and sustain social cohesion.
